heading: The question has a trivial answer and a hard one
text: The research question asks whether a scientifically informed and partly mathematical framework can explain three things without pretending that love can be objectively measured: how care moves between people, where it becomes misaligned, and how misalignment reshapes relationships over time. Taken literally, the hypothesis "love intended ≠ love expressed ≠ love perceived ≠ love received ≠ relationship compatibility" cannot be false. No two psychological measurements correlate perfectly, so every "≠" is guaranteed by measurement error and by the general background correlation among psychological variables (the "crud factor") (Meehl 1990)

heading: The question has a trivial answer and a hard one
text: . A hypothesis that cannot lose tells us nothing. The methodological literature's remedy is to rewrite verbal claims as quantitative claims about named parameters, each with a pre-registered smallest effect of interest (Scheel et al. 2021; Lakens, Scheel & Isager 2018)

heading: Ten foundational questions, answered

heading: Ten foundational questions, answered
text: Is love expressed always recognizable as love? | No. Unambiguous support is read similarly by everyone, but ambiguous messages diverge by the receiver's attachment, and about half of sacrifices are missed. | Collins & Feeney 2004; Visserman et al. 2019

heading: Ten foundational questions, answered

heading: 3.1 Perceived responsiveness predicts well-being, but perceivers partly project it
text: Perceived partner responsiveness (PPR) is the sense that a partner understands, validates and cares for you. It is the central construct of the intimacy process model (Laurenceau, Barrett & Pietromonaco 1998) and has a validated self-report scale (Reis et al. 2017). In the largest pooled analysis of relationship predictors, 43 longitudinal dyadic datasets from 29 laboratories (11,196 couples), PPR was among the top relationship-specific predictors of relationship quality. It ranked behind perceived partner commitment, appreciation, sexual satisfaction and perceived partner satisfaction (Joel et al. 2020)

heading: 3.1 Perceived responsiveness predicts well-being, but perceivers partly project it
text: The health findings are smaller than often implied. In the US MIDUS cohort, PPR was measured with only three items (the partner cares, understands, appreciates). It predicted change in eudaimonic well-being over a decade (B = .057), not hedonic well-being (Selcuk et al. 2016). It explained about 2% of the variance in later cortisol slopes (Slatcher, Selcuk & Ong 2015). Its indirect path to mortality did not survive covariates (Stanton et al. 2019)

heading: 3.1 Perceived responsiveness predicts well-being, but perceivers partly project it
text: The finding that matters most for the hypothesis concerns where perceived responsiveness comes from. In dyadic marriage studies, a spouse's own responsiveness predicted their perception of the partner's responsiveness more strongly than the partner's self-reported responsiveness did. That held for global perceptions measured against the partner's self-report; in daily diaries, counts of benefits received tracked the partner's reported giving as much as one's own (.36 against .34). Experimentally making one's own past support feel harder to recall lowered perceived partner responsiveness (Lemay, Clark & Feeney 2007; Lemay & Clark 2008)

heading: 3.2 The intimacy process holds within moments but is untested as a causal chain
text: Diary studies support the model's core claim. In 96 married couples followed for 42 days, one's own disclosure and the partner's disclosure each predicted same-day intimacy, with perceived responsiveness as a partial mediator (Laurenceau, Barrett & Rovine 2005). Observer-coded responses to a partner's disclosures predicted relationship well-being and break-up two months later. Responses to good news were more predictive than responses to bad news (Gable, Gonzaga & Strachman 2006). Enthusiastic responses to shared good news increased trust in experiments with strangers (Reis et al. 2010)

heading: 3.5 Accuracy, bias and attribution: people are accurate and biased at once
text: Romantic perception is surprisingly accurate and biased. A meta-analysis distinguished tracking accuracy (whether judgments covary with a benchmark, usually the partner's self-report, across couples or items), r = .47 across 98 studies, from mean-level bias, r = .09 across 48 studies. A congruence (similarity) effect requires a joint pattern, each part estimated with its uncertainty: a_4 < 0; a_3 = 0; and the ridge on the line of congruence, that is a first principal axis with intercept p_{10} = 0 and slope p_{11} = 1 (equivalently a_5 = 0 given a_3 = 0) (Schönbrodt, Humberg & Nestler 2018; Humberg, Nestler & Back 2019)

heading: 8.7 Component 4: need fulfilment and fit
text: Empirical tests. Point estimates are not enough. The required evidence is confidence intervals (for example bootstrap) for a_3, a_4, p_{10} and p_{11}; comparison of the full quadratic model with constrained models such as the squared-difference model, which imposes b_1 = b_2 = 0, b_3 = b_5 and b_4 = -2b_3 (Edwards 2007); enough observations in incongruent regions that the surface is not extrapolated; and adequate power for quadratic terms. Moderated regression with main effects and a single interaction cannot represent a congruence effect (Schönbrodt, Humberg & Nestler 2018). Significance tests for the surface quantities should use the corrected formulas published in an erratum to Shanock et al. (2014; not accessed for this paper)

text: Each person's outcomes depend on both people. For distinguishable roles (parent and child; giver-role on a given day), the actor–partner interdependence model writes Y_A = a_A X_A + p_A X_B + e_A and Y_B = a_B X_B + p_B X_A + e_B with correlated errors (Cook & Kenny 2005)

heading: 8.11 Asymmetry and dyadic structure
text: The component of misperception that best matches "translation" is the relationship effect of the Social Relations Model. In X_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + \gamma_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}, \alpha_i is the perceiver's general tendency, \beta_j the target's general expressiveness, and \gamma_{ij} the pair-specific residual (Kenny & La Voie 1984). This cannot be identified within a single couple, because with two people the relationship effect is confounded with perceiver and target effects. It requires round-robin family designs, in which each member rates each other member, or people rating several partners, with at least two indicators (Cook 1994)

heading: 8.11 Asymmetry and dyadic structure
tag: Established method; no relationship application located
text: Channels are not independent, and their weights may change. Care channels co-vary: time together enables talk and touch, and money can buy time. A model that treats channels as orthogonal axes misstates their structure, so channel-level analyses need a measured covariance or latent-factor structure. Network models of how channels co-vary within couples are exploratory at best, given replicability concerns about such networks (Forbes et al. 2017). Whether a channel's importance changes over time can be estimated with time-varying effect models (Tan et al. 2012; Bringmann et al. 2017). Money might matter more during education, for example, and presence more during a crisis. Such models need long series and a prior theory of why weights should change, such as a developmental transition. Without both, time-varying weights simply overfit

heading: 8.11 Asymmetry and dyadic structure
text: The cross-channel translation matrix \boldsymbol{\Lambda} in \mathbf{S}_B = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\,\mathbf{E}_A would capture how much each act counts toward each need, for example how far money "counts" as time. It has K^2 parameters per dyad, 25 for five channels, and cannot be estimated per dyad from weeks of diaries. It needs pooling with structure (diagonal plus a few theorized off-diagonal terms) or within-dyad randomization of channels

heading: "90 versus 40" is a measurement problem before it is a psychological one
text: The brief's illustration is useful because it separates two sincere reports, but the two numbers are probably not answers to the same question. A giver's "I provided 90% of what was needed" is a judgment of adequacy relative to need. Over-claiming studies measure share of joint work (Ross & Sicoly 1979), and studies of recipients' reactions measure momentary feeling. Before calling a gap a translation failure, a study must put both people on the same construct, time frame and scale. On a 0–100 scale with a standard deviation near 20, a 50-point gap would be about 2.5 standard deviations (illustrative arithmetic), several times the mean-level gaps found in parent–child and couple research (g ≈ .2–.5; Hou et al. 2020; Korelitz & Garber 2016)

heading: Stereotypes fail, so averages must never describe individuals
text: Cultural stereotypes about care are unreliable. Using culture-specific items and response-set adjustment, Japanese respondents valued directly verbalizing feelings to mother and father more than Americans did, the opposite of the stereotype (Seki, Matsumoto & Imahori 2002). A meta-analysis found European Americans were not less collectivistic than Japanese or Koreans (Oyserman, Coon & Kemmelmeier 2002). Of 35 Japan–US comparisons, only five supported the textbook view (Takano & Osaka 2018). Countries agree more than they disagree on value priorities (Fischer & Schwartz 2011)

heading: Stereotypes fail, so averages must never describe individuals
text: Likert self-reports are distorted by reference-group effects, because people rate themselves relative to those around them (Heine et al. 2002). Cross-cultural mean comparisons therefore need measurement invariance, or a defensible alternative such as alignment (Asparouhov & Muthén 2014; Robitzsch & Lüdtke 2023). Most studies cited here did not report it

heading: What changes, and where the change happens
text: Within individuals, three things move. Needs change with development: parent–child conflict affect rises from early to middle adolescence (Laursen, Coy & Collins 1998), and personal-domain autonomy claims grow with age (Smetana & Asquith 1994). Attachment anxiety and avoidance decline across adulthood and with being in a relationship (Chopik, Edelstein & Grimm 2019). Relationship satisfaction follows age- and duration-linked trajectories, falling from 20 to 40 and in the first decade of a relationship (Bühler, Krauss & Orth 2021)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case A: perfect understanding, incompatible lives. In couples paged six times a day, closeness and well-being were highest when an activity served both partners' goals. Pursuing only the partner's goals was costly (Gere et al. 2011). Each partner's report of goal conflict was associated with lower relationship quality and well-being for both (Gere & Schimmack 2013)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case B: manipulative responsiveness. Self-interested actors can manufacture warmth. Narcissism's most exploitative facets were the most attractive at first sight (Back, Schmukle & Egloff 2010), and self-enhancers' early appeal faded within weeks (Paulhus 1998). Ingratiation reliably increases liking unless it is seen as transparent (Gordon 1996). Emotion-regulation knowledge amplified the link from Machiavellianism to interpersonal deviance (Côté et al. 2011). Affection made contingent on compliance predicted poorer relationship quality through frustrated autonomy (Kanat-Maymon et al. 2016)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Two caveats keep this case honest. No study has measured perceived partner responsiveness inside manipulative or abusive relationships. And "love bombing" has essentially no peer-reviewed evidence base. A PubMed title and abstract search run for this review in November 2026 returned no records, and a popular summary likewise notes that little peer-reviewed research exists (Psychology Today)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case C: love and abuse. Love, commitment and abuse coexist routinely. In a meta-synthesis of 282 women's accounts, early violence was discounted "for the sake of romantic commitment" (Kearney 2001). Among highly committed people, tolerance for a partner's aggression rose once it began; commitment was measured, not manipulated (Arriaga, Capezza & Daly 2016). People in aggressive relationships overestimated how unhappy a break-up would make them (Arriaga et al. 2013). Staying is predicted by poor economic alternatives and investments (Rusbult & Martz 1995)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Coercive control is linked to PTSD symptoms at r = .32 (Lohmann et al. 2024). Nonviolent coercive control produces fear comparable to violent intimate terrorism (Conroy & Crowley 2022). Lifetime physical or sexual partner violence affects about 27% of ever-partnered women aged 15–49 worldwide (Sardinha et al. 2022)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case D: parental love that violates autonomy. Sincere love combined with autonomy violation is the modal case, not the exception. Dependency-oriented psychological control is linked to parental separation anxiety, and achievement-oriented control to parental perfectionism (Soenens, Vansteenkiste & Luyten 2010). Mothers in four cultures, including Korean immigrant mothers, gave care-oriented reasons for control (Cho et al. 2021). Conditional regard achieves compliance at an emotional cost (Assor, Roth & Deci 2004)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Cultural normativeness reduces, sometimes; it does not remove the harm. Physical discipline predicted problems regardless of its normativeness (Lansford et al. 2005). Spanking effects did not differ by ethnicity in a US national sample of 11,044 (Gershoff et al. 2012). Children's own perceived normativeness buffered some effects in China (Liu & Wang 2018). The "tiger parenting" profile predicted worse, not better, outcomes for Chinese American youth (Kim et al. 2013b)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case E: good intentions, harmful outcomes. Forgiveness, positive expectations and benevolent attributions helped in healthy marriages but predicted worse outcomes in troubled ones (McNulty & Fincham 2012; McNulty, O'Mara & Karney 2008). A tendency to forgive predicted continued partner aggression (McNulty 2011). Accommodating a family member's anxiety maintains the problem: a parent-only programme that reduces accommodation was noninferior to child cognitive-behavioural therapy in a randomized trial (Lebowitz et al. 2020)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case F: unsustainable needs. Communal motivation of every kind predicted relationship well-being, but only non-unmitigated forms predicted the giver's personal well-being (Le et al. 2018). High unmitigated communion even predicted a slower decline in satisfaction over seven years (Horne, Impett & Johnson 2020), so the dyad looks healthy while the giver pays. Strained caregivers faced higher mortality risk (Schulz & Beach 1999), although caregiving overall was not harmful in population studies (Roth, Fredman & Haley 2015). Excessive reassurance seeking correlates with interpersonal rejection at r = .14 (Starr & Davila 2008)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case G: different but successful expressions. Spouses express love through partly different behaviours across 13 years of marriage. Wives showed it by enacting fewer negative behaviours, and husbands by initiating sex, shared leisure and joint housework (Schoenfeld, Bredow & Huston 2012). Couples build private idioms whose number tracks love and closeness (Bell, Buerkel-Rothfuss & Gore 1987) and a "shared reality" they defend under threat (Rossignac-Milon et al. 2021). Breadth of loving behaviour predicted quality better than any primary channel (Flicker, Sancier-Barbosa & Impett 2025)

heading: 15. Failure cases and counterexamples
text: Case H: stability without strong romantic love. Moral and structural commitment are distinct from personal, love-based commitment (Johnson, Caughlin & Huston 1999). Stable but unhappy marriages exist and carry costs to happiness, self-esteem and health (Hawkins & Booth 2005). About half of divorces in a US national sample ended low-distress marriages (Amato & Hohmann-Marriott 2007). Small selected samples of arranged marriages report satisfaction comparable to love marriages (Regan, Lakhanpal & Anguiano 2012), while larger probability samples in Chengdu and Nepal favour self-chosen marriage (Xu & Whyte 1990; Allendorf & Ghimire 2013)

heading: Designs and what each can establish
text: Dyadic daily diaries of four weeks or more identify detection, truth and bias for each link, multilevel response surfaces and within-dyad dynamics (Laurenceau & Bolger 2005). Three to four weeks is a practical minimum. It is enough to estimate average autoregressive and coupling parameters across many dyads but weak for any single dyad, and short series bias state-noise estimates (Song & Ferrer 2009). The number of days and dyads should be set by simulation (Schultzberg & Muthén 2018; Lafit et al. 2021)

heading: Designs and what each can establish
text: Within-person data are helpful but neither necessary nor sufficient for causal inference, because time-varying confounders produce spurious within-person associations (Rohrer & Murayama 2023). The classic cross-lagged panel model is "almost never the right choice" (Lucas 2023). The random-intercept version depends on parametric assumptions (Lüdtke & Robitzsch 2022)

heading: Ethical constraints
text: Couple and family research raises issues that standard regulations address poorly: confidentiality among members, consent with several members (including minors), shared data, harms to the family unit, and abuse reporting (Margolin et al. 2005)
